drapeaux.note: Traduite depuis le français ; l'original est un texte anglais de Franz Boas (rapport de 1910, cité dans Gravlee, Bernard & Leonard 2003) dont la formulation exacte est à retrouver. Le passage français « Le Hébreu d'Europe de l'Est » est une traduction de « the east European Hebrew ».

accroche: Measuring 17,821 New York immigrants between 1908 and 1910, an anthropologist discovers that skull shape is anything but fixed.
contenu_vulgarise:
New York, 1908. In an office rented near Ellis Island, a nine-year-old boy, born in Sicily, holds out his head to an assistant equipped with calipers. The instrument measures the width and length of the skull to the millimeter. Beside him, his mother waits her turn: she went through the same examination ten minutes earlier. Nothing sets the scene apart from a routine medical checkup. Yet it belongs to one of the largest anthropometric surveys ever carried out in the United States.

## A Number Supposed to Be Immutable

The anthropologist Franz Boas directed the operation on behalf of the Dillingham Commission, tasked by Congress with studying the mass immigration then underway. Between 1908 and 1910, he and thirteen assistants measured 17,821 immigrants and their children in New York: Eastern European Hebrews, Sicilians, Neapolitans, Bohemians, Poles, among other groups. They recorded height, weight, face width, and above all the cephalic index: the ratio of the width to the length of the skull. At the time, this index was regarded as a nearly permanent racial signature; Karl Pearson's physical anthropology built its classifications of human “types” on it.

## What the Child Does Not Keep

Boas compared the European-born parents with their children born in the United States. The result contradicted the starting hypothesis: skull shape changes, and changes fast, from one generation to the next. Among the children born in America, the gap between the groups of origin narrowed markedly compared with the one measured in their parents, with no biological mixing to explain the shift; the only thing that changes is where the child grows up. One generation is enough to erase part of what was presented as the biological foundation of race.

## A Debate That Is Still Not Closed

Boas published his results in 1911, then an expanded version in the American Anthropologist the following year. He saw in them proof that environment (diet, living conditions) shapes the body far more than the physical anthropology of his day admitted. Politically, though, the finding stopped nothing: the Commission that had commissioned it recommended immigration restrictions anyway, which would lead to the quota laws of 1921 and 1924. Boas's figures carried no weight in the decision they were meant to inform.

The scientific debate reopened a century later, and it is still not settled. In 2002, a statistical reanalysis by Corey Sparks and Richard Jantz concluded that the hereditary share of skull shape remains dominant, contradicting Boas. A year later, another team, Clarence Gravlee, Russell Bernard, and William Leonard, took the same data with more sophisticated methods and reached the opposite conclusion: Boas was right. What a caliper measured on the head of a Sicilian child in 1908 still occupies statisticians more than a century later.

citation.texte: The Eastern European Hebrew, who has a very round head, becomes more dolichocephalic; the Southern Italian, who in Italy has a very long head, becomes more brachycephalic — to the point that the two types approach a common form in this country, as far as the roundness of the skull is concerned.

carte.punch: A Sicilian child measured in 1908 still divides statisticians.
carte.idee: By measuring 17,821 New York immigrants between 1908 and 1910, Franz Boas shows that skull shape changes from one generation to the next, contradicting the idea of a fixed racial trait. Two modern reanalyses, in 2002 and 2003, reach opposite conclusions about his data.

quiz.question: Why does the narrowing of the cephalic index that Boas observed between parents and children pose a problem for the physical anthropology of his day?
choix: Because it proves that the measuring instruments used were poorly calibrated
Because this index was considered a stable racial trait, passed on unchanged
Because the families measured all belonged to the same group of origin
Because Boas had measured a sample judged too small to be significant
quiz.explication: The cephalic index served as the basis for the racial classifications of physical anthropology, which were supposed to reflect fixed traits passed down from generation to generation. Seeing it vary within a single generation, with no biological change, undermined that hypothesis; it was not an instrument problem, nor a homogeneous or too-small sample.

quiz_supplementaire.question: How many people did Franz Boas and his assistants measure between 1908 and 1910?
choix: About 900 immigrants, a sample judged small
quiz_supplementaire.explication: Boas and thirteen assistants measured 17,821 immigrants and their children in New York between 1908 and 1910, one of the largest anthropometric surveys ever carried out in the United States.

quiz_supplementaire.question: What decision did the Dillingham Commission make despite Boas's results?
choix: It funded a second study to verify the results
It asked for Boas to be removed from the commission
It filed the report away without any public follow-up
quiz_supplementaire.explication: The Commission that had commissioned the study nonetheless recommended immigration restrictions, which led to the quota laws of 1921 and 1924: Boas's figures carried no weight in the decision.

quiz_supplementaire.question: What do the two statistical reanalyses of Boas's data carried out in 2002 and 2003 show?
choix: Both confirm that Boas was mistaken
They reach conclusions opposed to each other
They could not be carried out for lack of surviving data
quiz_supplementaire.explication: In 2002, Sparks and Jantz concluded that the hereditary share dominates, contradicting Boas; in 2003, Gravlee, Bernard, and Leonard took the same data and concluded the opposite: Boas was right.
